overview: The Bahamas became independent in 1973 after a much longer history of Lucayan communities, colonial settlement, slavery and struggles for political rights. Pottery, house yards and living craft traditions reveal how people worked, raised families and made things together across the islands.

periods.title: Lucayan island communities
periods.summary: Lucayan communities made shell-tempered pottery and adapted technologies to limestone islands within a wider Caribbean world. This approximate phase is not an exact first-arrival date.

periods.title: European contact and colonial disruption
periods.summary: European arrival brought capture, enslavement and disease that devastated Lucayan communities. Later European settlement transformed the islands again.

periods.title: Royal colony and plantation expansion
periods.summary: Woodes Rogers became royal governor in 1718. Loyalists arriving after the American Revolution brought enslaved people and expanded plantation settlement.

periods.title: Abolition and compulsory apprenticeship
periods.summary: The abolition law took effect in 1834, but compulsory apprenticeship continued until 1838.

periods.title: Emancipation and unequal political rights
periods.summary: Apprenticeship ended in 1838. The struggle to widen political participation continued; women first voted in a general election in 1962.

periods.title: Women enter the electorate
periods.summary: Women voted in the November 1962 election after years of organizing and petitions. Majority rule followed in 1967.

periods.title: Majority rule before independence
periods.summary: The 1967 election led to a PLP government supported by Labour and an independent member. This political transition preceded national independence.

periods.title: The independent Bahamas
periods.summary: Independence on 10 July 1973 followed an election mandate and constitutional negotiations involving government and opposition delegates.

sections.title: Discoveries: clay, weaving and island food

items.text: A pottery recipe began with a surprising ingredient: dust blown across the Atlantic from the Sahara. Researchers sampled red deposits on Long Island and experimented with Palmetto Ware, the Lucayan pottery containing burned, crushed conch shell. The shell helped difficult local material hold its shape. Experiments indicate relatively low firing temperatures, showing careful adaptation to the islands’ available resources.

At Long Bay on San Salvador, impressions preserved in pottery reveal woven materials that have largely decayed. Hutcheson’s study compares these with other Late Lucayan sites; at Palmetto Grove, impressions even preserve evidence of woven spun thread. Clay kept a record of fibre work. Different patterns suggest variation in craft, but do not automatically identify a specific ethnic group.

At Clifton on New Providence, excavators distinguished two Lucayan settlements using radiocarbon dates and objects, rather than assuming all nearby remains belonged to one village. Griddles, hollow vessels, shell beads and tools differed between the sites. Marine remains show the importance of conch and other seafood. The researchers favoured successive settlement over a long-lived pair of simultaneous villages.

Laundry left clues at early nineteenth-century Clifton. Buttons, beads and fasteners clustered between houses and outdoor kitchens; the excavators interpreted them as losses during washing and drying. Food remains and cooking tools marked other activity areas. The yards supported sewing, childcare and conversation as well as chores, within the constrained lives of enslaved households.

On Cat Island, Iva Thompson passed skills to her family, including Sheena Woodside and Peggy Johnson. The tourism ministry’s family profile describes Woodside plaiting dried palm leaves into bags, baskets and rugs from childhood. Ordinary plants became useful household objects through learned patterns and patient hands. This is one documented family’s story, not a rule for every Bahamian home.

The same Cat Island family remembers bush teas made from local plants, including cerasee, breadfruit and guava. Peggy Johnson describes this knowledge as part of an inherited tradition of care. The account tells us what this family practised and valued; it does not demonstrate that a tea cures an illness.

sections.title: Making music, costumes and public memory

items.text: For Junkanoo, families and groups transform cardboard and crepe paper into towering costumes. Skills pass between generations in preparation spaces called shacks and at home. A child can learn by helping someone who already knows the craft. UNESCO’s 2023 inscription recognizes the shared work and creativity behind the spectacle.

The street music of Junkanoo includes whistles, cowbells, horns and goatskin drums. A 2022 postal-service account describes months of preparation and costumes whose materials changed over time, from cloth and natural materials to elaborate cardboard constructions. The exact origin remains debated. The parade is the part you see; much of the work happens beforehand.

At Clifton, Antonius Roberts carved female figures from unwanted casuarina tree trunks, leaving them in place as a memorial. Tyrone Ferguson added metal bells. The work, called Sacred Space, connects art, ancestry and the landscape. These contemporary sculptures commemorate history; they are not excavated Lucayan statues.

The Burma Road unrest of 1942 grew from workers’ anger over unequal pay at an airfield construction project. Bahamian labourers learned that Americans received more for comparable work. The dispute helped connect workplace demands with the wider struggle over racial inequality and political power.

Mary Ingraham, Doris Johnson, Eugenia Lockhart and other campaigners pressed for women’s voting rights through organizing and petitions. Women voted in the general election of 26 November 1962. That achievement widened participation before majority rule in 1967.

After the September 1972 election, the Bahamas legislature requested independence and government and opposition delegates attended a London conference. The resulting settlement fixed 10 July 1973 as independence day. This was a negotiated end to British colonial rule, not a conquest or the disappearance of an island community.

ending.text: British colonial rule ended with independence in 1973. The Bahamas continues as a country. The map’s separate entries represent coverage of the same islands, not vanished and refounded societies.
